title: TCP connection and TLS handshake
description: Learn how TCP establishes connections, how the TLS handshake secures them, and why both stages affect page load speed and security.

data.text: Once DNS gives your browser an IP address, the next step is opening a connection. On the public internet, that almost always means **TCP**, and almost always means **TLS** on top of it. Together, these two handshakes can add hundreds of milliseconds before a single byte of application data is sent.
TCP guarantees that bytes arrive in order and without corruption. It does this using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmissions. For web traffic, TCP is the default transport protocol.

data.title: TCP three-way handshake
items: Connection is open; application data can flow.

data.title: Latency note
data.text: A full TCP handshake requires one round-trip before data can start. On high-latency networks, that cost is noticeable.

TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts traffic between client and server. Without TLS, anyone on the network path can read or modify requests and responses. Modern browsers mark non-HTTPS sites as 'Not secure'.

items: TLS 1.2 is still common but considered aging
TLS 1.3 is faster and more secure; most production servers should use it
Certificates bind a public key to a domain name
Certificate Authorities (CAs) issue and verify certificates

data.text: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake to a single round-trip for new connections and zero round-trips for resumed connections. It also removes older, insecure cipher suites and features.

data.title: TLS 1.3 abbreviated handshake
items: Client sends ClientHello with supported cipher suites.
Server replies with ServerHello, certificate, and Finished.
Client verifies and sends its Finished.

data.caption: TCP plus TLS handshake combined timeline
data.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Browser
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: TCP SYN
    S->>C: SYN-ACK
    C->>S: ACK
    C->>S: TLS ClientHello
    S->>C: TLS ServerHello + Certificate
    C->>S: TLS Finished
    S->>C: TLS Finished
    Note over C,S: Encrypted HTTP request begins

data.title: TLS pitfalls
data.text: Expired certificates, mismatched domain names, or incomplete certificate chains will cause browsers to block the connection. Always validate your certificate chain with tools like SSL Labs.
Browsers reuse connections through HTTP keep-alive. Opening a new TCP+TLS connection for every request is expensive; persistent connections let multiple requests share the same handshake cost.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery via a three-way handshake.
TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake to one round-trip for new connections.
Certificate issues are a common cause of hard-to-debug connection failures.
Connection reuse through keep-alive is essential for performance.
data.takeaway: TCP and TLS are the foundation of every secure web request. Understanding their handshakes explains much of the latency and security behavior you observe in production.

items.question: Why does HTTPS feel slower than HTTP sometimes?
items.answer: TLS adds handshake latency and encryption overhead. With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and TLS 1.3, the difference is usually small. Often the real cause is server performance, not encryption.

items.question: What is session resumption in TLS?
items.answer: TLS can reuse earlier cryptographic parameters to skip part or all of the handshake. Session tickets and session IDs let clients reconnect faster without a full handshake.

items.question: Can I use TCP without TLS?
items.answer: Yes, but browsers enforce HTTPS for most production features. HTTP over plain TCP is still used internally or in controlled environments.

data.text: TLS 1.3 is not just more secure; it is measurably faster because it removes obsolete negotiation steps.
